title: Jainism: the path of non-violence
examples: Why do Jains not eat root vegetables?

explain.say: Jainism is an ancient religion of India. Jains follow the teachings of twenty-four great teachers called tirthankaras, the last of whom was Mahavira, who lived about 2,500 years ago, at the same time as the Buddha.

explain.say: Jains take five vows: non-violence, truthfulness, not stealing, chastity, and non-attachment to things. Monks and nuns keep them fully, and lay Jains keep gentler versions.

explain.say: This shapes daily life. Jains are vegetarian, many avoid root vegetables so the whole plant and tiny creatures are not killed, and some monks sweep the path softly to avoid stepping on insects.

Jains also teach anekantavada, the many sidedness of truth: like blind people each touching one part of an elephant, everyone sees only part of reality. There are two main groups, Digambara and Shvetambara.

items: Digambara: sky clad, monks wear no clothes
Shvetambara: monks and nuns wear white

draw.a: Truth has many sides: listen to other views

faq.a: Ahimsa means non-violence: not harming any living being in thought, word or action. It is the most important teaching of Jainism, and is also valued in Hinduism and Buddhism. Mahatma Gandhi made it famous worldwide.

Mahavira was the twenty-fourth and last tirthankara of this age, born a prince in what is now Bihar, India, about 2,500 years ago. He gave up his riches, lived as a monk, reached perfect knowledge and taught the Jain path.

A tirthankara, or ford maker, is a great teacher who has crossed the river of rebirth to liberation and shows others how. Jains honour twenty-four tirthankaras in this age, from Rishabhanatha to Mahavira.

faq.q: What are the five vows of Jainism?
faq.a: The five vows are ahimsa, non-violence; satya, truthfulness; asteya, not stealing; brahmacharya, chastity and self-control; and aparigraha, non-attachment to possessions. Monks and nuns keep them fully, lay people more gently.

faq.q: Why do Jains not eat root vegetables?
faq.a: Many Jains avoid onions, garlic, potatoes and carrots because pulling them up kills the whole plant, and harms the many tiny creatures living in the soil. It comes from their deep commitment to ahimsa.
asks: Why no onions and garlic for Jains?

faq.a: Jains do not believe in a creator god. They believe the universe has always existed. They honour the tirthankaras, perfected souls who show the path, and each soul can itself become perfect and free.
asks: Is there a god in Jainism?

faq.a: Jains see karma as a fine, invisible matter that sticks to the soul when we act with anger, greed or harm, and weighs it down in the cycle of rebirth. Right living, fasting and meditation help remove it.

faq.q: Why do some Jain monks cover their mouths?
faq.a: Some Jain monks and nuns wear a small cloth over their mouth to avoid harming tiny living things in the air, and carry a soft brush to sweep insects gently from their path. It is ahimsa in practice.
asks: Why do Jains wear a mask?
Why do Jain monks carry a broom?

faq.q: What is the difference between Digambara and Shvetambara?
faq.a: They are the two main Jain groups. Digambara, meaning sky clad, monks wear no clothes as a sign of total non-attachment. Shvetambara, meaning white clad, monks and nuns wear simple white robes.

Anekantavada means many sidedness: the idea that truth is complex and no single view sees all of it. Jains tell of blind people touching different parts of an elephant, each sure they know what it is.
asks: Blind men and elephant story meaning

faq.q: What are the Three Jewels of Jainism?
faq.a: The Three Jewels are right faith, right knowledge and right conduct. Together they form the path to liberation, called moksha, the freeing of the soul from karma and rebirth.
asks: What is the Jain path to liberation?

faq.a: Paryushana is the most important Jain festival, a time of fasting, prayer and reflection lasting eight or ten days. It ends with asking forgiveness from everyone, with the words Michchhami Dukkadam.
asks: What is the main Jain festival?

faq.a: There are about 4 to 5 million Jains, most of them in India, especially in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra and Karnataka. Smaller communities live in the UK, the USA, Kenya and elsewhere.

facts: Mahavira was the 24th tirthankara of Jainism and lived about 2,500 years ago, around the same time as the Buddha.
The five Jain vows are ahimsa, satya, asteya, brahmacharya and aparigraha.
The two main Jain groups are Digambara and Shvetambara.
The statue of Bahubali at Shravanabelagola, about 17 metres tall, was carved from a single rock over a thousand years ago.
Jains do not believe in a creator god.

quiz.say: Two friends disagree, and a Jain says each of them sees part of the truth. Which Jain idea is this?

quiz.why: Anekantavada, the many sidedness of truth, teaches that reality is complex and different views can each hold part of it.
